source.title: Data augmentation instead of explicit regularization

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares true-label test performance with and without explicit regularization, bearing on V5's claim about removing regularization. It does not test fitting random labels.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on true-label generalization with weight decay, dropout and data augmentation. It does not apply random labels, shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs, or measure learning order. Cited findings about random-label fitting are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V5's true-label generalization clause by removing weight decay and dropout, with and without augmentation. It does not test random-label fitting or V1–V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that augmentation can match or exceed the generalization benefits of weight decay and dropout, whose unchanged hyperparameters transfer poorly across data amounts and architectures. They acknowledge that carefully tuned weight decay and dropout can still improve performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains standard image-classification networks on true labels while varying weight decay, dropout and data augmentation; it does not use the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with data augmentation level, training-data amount, architecture depth, and whether weight decay and dropout are included.

fits_no_version.finding: Without weight decay and dropout, validation accuracy rises faster and depends less on learning-rate decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing weight decay and dropout can accelerate true-label validation learning under the tested schedules.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight norms vary with augmentation, regularization, and batch normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These training choices affect learned weight norms; norms alone do not explain the reported accuracy differences.

record.problems: The authors note a limited number of experiments (over 300 models). Several comparisons are aggregates across architectures and datasets; the results concern image categorization with the tested architectures and settings.

untested.parts: All parts: random-label training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training time for random versus true labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across random-label corruption fractions.
Whether regularization prevents fitting random labels. Removal of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation is evaluated jointly; their separate necessity is not comprehensively isolated.
Learning real-label patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

missing.what: Absolute full-data accuracies and matched regularization comparisons, including bare models and models without batch normalization. For example, All-CNN/CIFAR-100 without batch normalization achieves 60.54% with weight decay and dropout but no augmentation, versus 39.03% with all three removed. Preserve model-specific comparisons rather than only aggregate gains.

Reduced-data results without augmentation: at 50% data, unregularized and regularized models retain 88.11% and 83.20%; at 10%, 58.72% and 58.75%. These directly address removal of all three techniques.

Additional 80% and 1% data comparisons, including exceptions at 1%: DenseNet/CIFAR-10 with light augmentation reaches 41.85% without regularization versus 48.12% with it. Authors explicitly caution about greater variability at 1%.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its definition treats augmentation as implicit regularization, whereas V5 includes augmentation among the techniques being removed. Retaining augmentation therefore tests only part of V5. Reduced-data and changed-depth advantages support nonnecessity; they are not themselves scope limitations.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting, chance test error, and whether fitting requires changes to architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time for true versus random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across fractions of randomly corrupted labels.

Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent fitting random labels. The study tests true-label generalization when weight decay and dropout are removed, in visual object categorization models.
Whether networks learn real-label patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

rows.operation_detail: Train without weight decay or dropout, with data augmentation; compared with models trained with both explicit regularizers and the same augmentation level.

conditions.value: paired comparison across architectures and data sets; 9/16 cases favor no explicit regularization

rows.measure: Test accuracy improvement over the bare-bone baseline (%)
rows.baseline: models trained with the same augmentation and with weight decay and dropout: mean 7.90 (4.03) across light and heavier augmentation; specific paired values vary
rows.value: Mean 8.57% for data augmentation alone; higher than the regularized model in 9/16 cases
rows.uncertainty: bootstrap analysis: difference positive with 95% confidence; P value = 0.0220
rows.note: The reported mean combines light and heavier augmentation; the study says the no-explicit-regularization models were better in more than half, not all, paired cases.
rows.check: V5 does not require removing regularization to improve every model. Comparable performance, with higher accuracy in 9/16 cases, supports nonnecessity. The stated SD 4.03 belongs to heavier augmentation with regularization, not the combined 7.90 mean.

source_check.correct: The baseline for the reported 8.57% improvement is the corresponding model without weight decay, dropout or augmentation. Improvement is 100 × (accuracy − baseline)/accuracy. rows.baseline: models with weight decay and dropout
rows.value: Models without explicit regularization performed on average 11.23% better (SD = 3.06)
rows.note: The study says regularized models suffered a dramatic drop after architecture changes; the no-explicit-regularization models changed less.
